content: Sickle cell disease is a prevalent genetic disorder characterized by episodes of pain, known as sickle cell crises. These crises occur when abnormally shaped and dehydrated red blood cells obstruct blood vessels. Current treatment approaches are primarily supportive and symptomatic. Laboratory studies on piracetam suggest that it may inhibit or reverse the sickling process of red blood cells. This review is an update of a previously published Cochrane review. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of piracetam in reducing the frequency of painful sickle cell crises. To achieve this, a search was conducted in the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register, which includes references from extensive electronic database searches and manual reviews of relevant journals and conference proceedings. The last search of this register was performed on September 21, 2015. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared orally administered piracetam to either a placebo or standard care in individuals of all ages and sexes with sickle cell disease. Two authors independently assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. Additional information was sought from the trial authors, and data on adverse effects were collected from the studies. Three trials, involving a total of 169 participants, were included in the review. However, the data provided were limited, incomplete, and based on unvalidated assumptions. One trial reported a reduction in the frequency and severity of pain crises with piracetam compared to placebo, but no supporting data were presented to confirm these findings. Another trial provided a monthly global pain score based on the number and severity of sickle cell crises but did not present separate data for these primary outcomes. In one trial, there was no significant difference between piracetam and placebo in the number of days participants were hospitalized (P = 0.87). However, inconsistencies in the criteria for hospitalization during sickle cell crises made it difficult to draw reliable conclusions. Two trials reported participant satisfaction with piracetam, but no details were provided on how this satisfaction was measured. There were no reports of toxicity or adverse effects associated with piracetam, except for one participant who experienced dizziness. The authors concluded that the small number of included trials and their poor methodological quality do not provide sufficient reliable evidence to support the routine use of piracetam for preventing painful sickle cell crises. While searches for potentially relevant trials will continue, the authors do not plan to update other sections of the review unless new trials are published.
